newsitem.title: USA: Michigan Gov. declares emergency following storms.
newsitem.headline: Michigan Gov. declares emergency following storms.

text.p: Violent storms and tornadoes killed at least seven people, including five members of one Michigan family, injured dozens more and battered parts of three Midwest states, authorities said on Thursday.

Michigan Gov. John Engler declared a state of emergency and asked for federal disaster assistance to help recover from widespread destruction caused by winds of up to 100 mph (160 kph) that swept through on Wednesday afternoon.

"We're also activating the National Guard to help the clean-up effort because that is a mission they have handled effectively in the past," the Republican governor said after touring some of the hardest-hit areas.
The powerful summer storm was particularly deadly for one family on an outing in Grosse Point Farms on Lake St. Clair near Detroit.

Police had warned about 400 people in Pier Park about the approaching storm, but family patriarch Abdo Algahim and about a dozen other family members stayed behind to clean up picnic debris. As the skies darkened, they huddled under a gazebo for shelter but high winds that may have actually been a tornado swept them and the structure into the lake.

Algahim, 55, was listed in good condition with a fractured rib and collapsed lung. Killed were his wife Asma, 55, son Mohamed, 1; daughter Rukia, three months; sister-in-law Nabiha, about 30; and Nabiha's son Zakria, 10. Seven other children in the extended family were also hurt.

A suspected tornado crushed a mobile home and killed another person in Oakland County, where officials originally suspected a second death had occurred. Another person was killed in Flint, Michigan, by a falling tree.
The line of storms also spawned violent weather and tornados in Indiana and Ohio, although state officials reported no deaths or serious injuries.

Five homes were destroyed in Madison County in central Indiana and 30 others were damaged. Several homes were heavily damaged in Clermont County in southeast Ohio where a tornado skipped along a 10-mile (15 km) path. Electrical power and telephone service was also knocked out in some areas.

Michigan officials said a total of 105 people in five counties were injured, 42 of them in the city of Detroit. Across the state 84 homes were destroyed, more than 400 homes and businesses were damaged and 350 people were left homeless.
Detroit Mayor Dennis Archer said that after the storms passed the city remained relatively quiet, but warned that any looters would be dealt with harshly.

In Plymouth, west of Detroit in Oakland County, a local courthouse was destroyed by a raging fire caused by downed power lines. In Hamtramck, a working-class community bordering Detroit, roofs were torn off entire blocks of homes. Trees were uprooted and shattered glass littered streets.
"We got hit pretty hard. In all my years in Hamtramck I've never seen anything like this," said Mayor Robert Kozaren. "It's a complete disaster."

Detroit Edison Co. said about 280,000 people were still without power nearly a day after the storms hit. Outages knocked out roadway pumps, which led to flooding and traffic snarls throughout the area on Thursday morning.
